name: Design a Document Database
intent: Store flexible JSON documents with fast queries on any field, survive the loss of a machine without losing acknowledged writes, and spread a very large collection across many machines.
codeTitle: a replica set that survives its primary
finalIntro: One order being written with majority durability, and the primary dying right afterwards.
prompt: Design a document database like MongoDB. Applications store JSON-like documents of different shapes in collections and query them by many fields. It must stay available when a server dies, never lose a write that it has acknowledged as durable, and grow past what one machine can hold.
functional: Insert, read, update and delete documents that are nested JSON with arrays
Query by any field, sort, and page through results
Secondary indexes on one field and on several fields, including fields inside arrays
Allow documents in one collection to have different shapes, with optional validation rules
Update one document atomically, including changes to its nested fields
Let the application choose how safe each write must be and where each read comes from
nonFunctional: Reads and writes by key or by an indexed field take a few milliseconds
An acknowledged majority write is never lost, even if the primary dies at once
A failed primary is replaced in about 10 to 12 seconds with no manual action
Scale to billions of documents and tens of thousands of writes per second
No single shard takes a disproportionate share of the traffic
Adding a field or an index must not need downtime

firstAttempt.text: One server. Each document is serialised as JSON text and stored in a file or in a table with one text column. A query reads every document, parses it and tests the condition. For speed, the whole collection is also kept in memory.
limits: Every query that is not by key scans and parses the whole collection
An update rewrites the whole text, and a crash in the middle can leave a half-written file
There is no index on any field inside the documents
Anything can be stored, so a typing mistake in a field name quietly corrupts the data
When the one server dies, the database is down and the latest writes may be gone
A collection larger than one disk or one memory cannot be stored at all

steps.title: Store documents in a storage engine with a journal
steps.problem: Parsing text files on every query is slow, and a crash in the middle of a write can corrupt the data.
steps.fix: Put the documents in a real storage engine. Each document is stored in a compact binary form such as BSON, which keeps types like dates and integers, under a unique _id in a B-tree (WiredTiger in MongoDB) that is compressed on disk. An update changes one document under document-level concurrency control with multi-version reads, so readers never wait for writers. Every change is first written to a journal, a write-ahead log that is flushed every 100 ms or on request, and the data files are checkpointed about once a minute. After a crash the engine replays the journal from the last checkpoint.
steps.tradeoff: Reads by _id take one tree lookup, writes survive a crash, and readers and writers on different documents do not block each other. A document is rewritten as a whole when it grows, there is a 16 MiB size limit per document, and anything not yet journalled in the last 100 ms can be lost if the machine dies.

steps.title: Add secondary and compound indexes
steps.problem: Finding the orders of one customer from last week still scans every document, because only _id is indexed.
steps.fix: Let the application create B-tree indexes on other fields. An index maps field values to the document locations, and a compound index on several fields, such as customer then date, is sorted by the first field, then by the second. The rule of thumb for a compound index is equality fields first, then the sort field, then range fields. An index on an array field becomes a multikey index with one entry per element, a partial index covers only the matching documents, and a TTL index deletes documents when they expire. The query planner tries candidate indexes, caches the winner, and a query that needs only indexed fields is answered from the index alone.
steps.tradeoff: Queries on the indexed fields drop from a scan to a few page reads. Every index must be updated by every insert and by every update to its fields, costs memory, and a query only uses the leftmost fields of a compound index, so ten careless indexes can slow writes more than they speed reads.

steps.title: Allow flexible schemas, and validate what matters
steps.problem: Documents of different shapes are the point of the system, but a missing field or a price stored as text breaks the code that reads it, and the application has to decide how to model related data.
steps.fix: Keep the collection schema-free by default and add optional validation rules, written as JSON Schema, that the server checks on every insert and update, with a choice to reject or only warn. Evolve shapes gradually: new code writes a version field and old documents are upgraded lazily on read or by a background job. For related data, embed things that are read together and bounded in number, such as the lines of an order, because one document is read and updated atomically in one operation. Reference things that grow without limit, are shared, or change independently, such as a customer's thousands of orders, by storing their _id and fetching them with a second query or a lookup.
steps.tradeoff: A change of shape needs no migration and no downtime, and an embedded read is a single lookup. The database no longer enforces joins or foreign keys, so referenced data can dangle. An embedded array that grows without limit eventually hits the 16 MiB cap, and copying data into many documents makes changing it expensive.

steps.title: Run each data set as a replica set with elections
steps.problem: One server is a single point of failure, and a disk failure loses the data for good.
steps.fix: Keep the data on a replica set of an odd number of nodes, usually three. One node is the primary and takes all writes, and every write is also recorded as an entry in the oplog, a capped log that the secondaries copy and apply in the same order. Nodes send heartbeats every 2 seconds. If the primary is silent for the election timeout of 10 seconds, a secondary starts an election in a new term, in the style of Raft, and asks the others for votes. A node votes only for a candidate whose oplog is at least as up to date as its own, so a winner always holds every write that a majority has. The old primary rolls back any entries that never reached a majority when it returns.
steps.tradeoff: The set tolerates one lost node out of three, or two out of five, with no manual action and a gap of about 10 to 12 seconds with no primary. Two nodes cannot form a safe majority, so a small set needs a third voting member. Writes that only the old primary had are rolled back, and secondaries read old data by the length of their replication lag.

steps.title: Let each operation choose its write concern and read preference
steps.problem: Waiting for every replica makes every write slow, and acknowledging after the primary alone can lose a write at failover. Different data needs different guarantees.
steps.fix: A write concern says how many nodes must have the write before the client is told. w:1 waits for the primary only, w:majority waits until most voting nodes have it and journalled it, which is the default for most deployments, and a timeout turns a stuck write into an error rather than a hang. A read concern says what the data may be: local returns what this node has, majority returns only data that a majority has, so it cannot be rolled back. A read preference says where to read: primary for fresh data, secondary or nearest for slightly old data at lower cost. Retryable writes carry a transaction id so that a retry after a failover is applied once, and causal sessions let a client read its own writes from a secondary.
steps.tradeoff: The application pays for safety only where it needs it: majority for payments, w:1 for a click counter, secondary reads for dashboards. A majority write takes a round trip to the nearest secondary, and reading from secondaries returns stale data and can double the load on a set whose secondaries are already busy.

steps.title: Shard the collection by a well-chosen shard key
steps.problem: A replica set still stores all the data on every node, and one primary takes all the writes. A collection of billions of documents and 50,000 writes per second does not fit.
steps.fix: Split the collection into chunks by a shard key and spread the chunks over several shards, each a replica set. Query routers keep a copy of the chunk map from the config servers and send each operation to the right shard, or to all shards when the filter does not include the key. A balancer moves chunks of about 128 MB between shards to even out size, and a chunk is split in two when it grows. Choose the key for high cardinality, even writes and targeted queries: a hashed key spreads writes evenly but scatters range queries, a compound key with a customer prefix keeps one customer together, and an ever-increasing key such as a timestamp sends every insert to the last chunk, one hot shard.
steps.tradeoff: Capacity and write throughput grow by adding shards, and queries with the key touch one shard. A bad shard key is expensive to fix, because data must be moved (resharding is possible but heavy). Queries without the key hit every shard, multi-shard transactions need two-phase commit, and a single huge customer can still make one chunk too large to split.

failures.scenario: The primary dies right after acknowledging a w:1 write
failures.impact: The write is on the old primary only. The new primary does not have it, and when the old node returns it rolls the write back, so the client was told that it succeeded and it is gone.
failures.answer: Use w:majority for any write that matters. A majority write is acknowledged only after most nodes have it, so by the voting rule every possible winner holds it. Keep w:1 for data that can be lost, such as counters, and use retryable writes so the client can try again safely.

failures.scenario: All new orders go to one shard because the key is the order timestamp
failures.impact: Each insert has a larger key than the last, so they all fall in the last chunk on one shard. That shard is saturated and the other shards are idle, while the balancer keeps moving full chunks away.
failures.answer: Choose a key that spreads the inserts: hash the _id, or use customer id with a hashed or random suffix. If range queries by time are needed, bucket them by day on a secondary index or use zones, not by making time the shard key.

failures.scenario: An embedded array grows for ever
failures.impact: A document that gets a new comment or event on every action grows towards the 16 MiB limit. Every update rewrites more data, indexes on the array grow, and at the limit the update fails.
failures.answer: Bound what is embedded. Keep the last few items inside the document and store the rest as separate documents that reference the parent, or put them in buckets of fixed size. Alert on document size and array length before the limit.

failures.scenario: Dashboards read from a secondary that is lagging by minutes
failures.impact: Reports show old data, and a user who just saved a change does not see it on the next page if that read goes to a lagging secondary.
failures.answer: Monitor replication lag and take lagging members out of read rotation with a maximum staleness setting. Read what the user just wrote from the primary or in a causally consistent session, and use secondaries only for reads that can be a little old.

failures.scenario: A network partition leaves the primary with a minority of the nodes
failures.impact: The two nodes on the other side elect a new primary. The old primary is still running and thinks it is in charge, so a client connected to it could write to a node that will be rolled back.
failures.answer: A primary that cannot reach a majority steps down within the election timeout and stops accepting writes. Writes with w:majority to the isolated primary time out, never acknowledge, and the term number makes the old primary's entries lose.

alternatives.title: Embed or reference related data

options.name: Embed
options.pro: One read and one atomic update for the whole aggregate
options.con: Document growth, duplicated data, and the 16 MiB limit

options.name: Reference by _id
options.pro: Small documents, no duplication, independent updates
options.con: A second query or lookup, and no foreign keys to stop dangling references

alternatives.pick: Embed what is read together and bounded, such as order lines. Reference what is large, shared or unbounded, such as a customer's orders.

alternatives.title: The shard key

options.name: Ranged on a natural field
options.con: Increasing values and popular values create hot shards

options.name: Hashed
options.con: Range queries and queries by another field go to every shard

options.name: Compound with a prefix
options.pro: Queries for one tenant target one shard, and a suffix can split big tenants
options.con: Needs a thought-through second field, and prefix queries only

alternatives.pick: A compound key of the tenant or customer and a hashed or high-cardinality field, unless the workload is plain key lookups, when a hashed _id is enough.

alternatives.title: Write concern

options.name: w:1
options.pro: The lowest latency and the highest throughput
options.con: An acknowledged write can be rolled back at a failover

options.name: w:majority
options.pro: Survives the loss of any minority, with no rollback of acknowledged writes
options.con: Waits for a replica, and stalls if the majority is unreachable

options.name: w:all
options.con: One slow or dead node blocks every write

alternatives.pick: w:majority by default, and w:1 only where losing a recent write is acceptable.

alternatives.title: Document store or relational database

options.name: Document database
options.pro: Flexible shapes, aggregates in one document, and a simple route to sharding
options.con: Weaker joins, and consistency across documents is the application's job

options.name: Relational database
options.con: Schema changes and horizontal scaling take more effort

alternatives.pick: A document store when data is naturally nested, read as a whole and varied in shape. Relational when relationships and constraints dominate.

roles.label: Applications
roles.description: The services and jobs that read and write documents.

roles.label: Query layer
roles.description: The server or the router that parses and routes operations.

roles.label: Background movers
roles.description: The balancer that moves chunks between shards.

roles.label: Rules
roles.description: Schema validation rules checked on each write.

roles.label: State
roles.description: Storage engines, journals, indexes, replicas and config servers.

quiz.question: A query finds a customer's orders where total is above 100, sorted by createdAt newest first. The collection has 200 million documents. Which compound index serves the filter and the sort without sorting in memory?
options: customerId, then createdAt, then total, so the scan follows the sort order and filters on total
customerId, then total, then createdAt, so the range filter on total narrows the scan first
total, then customerId, then createdAt, so that the most selective field is the first key
createdAt, then customerId, then total, so that the newest orders are read first
quiz.explanation: Equality field first, then the sort field, then the range field, so the index already returns the orders in date order. Putting the range field before the sort field breaks the order and forces an in-memory sort.

quiz.question: A device document embeds every sensor reading in an array. A reading takes about 300 bytes and each device sends one per second. The size cap is 16 MiB and compression is ignored. What happens and what is the right model?
options: The cap is hit in about 15 days, so start a new device document each month and keep the arrays inside them
The cap is hit in about 15 hours, so raise the limit in the server settings above 16 MiB for this collection
The cap is hit in about 15 hours, so keep readings in separate bucket documents, such as one per hour
The cap is hit in about 15 hours, so store each reading as a JSON string in one long text field instead
quiz.explanation: 16 MiB divided by 300 bytes is about 56,000 readings, or roughly 15 hours at one per second. The limit is fixed, and a long text field has the same size, so unbounded data belongs in separate bucketed documents that reference the device.

quiz.question: A payments service uses a 3-node replica set and writes with w:1 plus journaling on the primary. The primary crashes just after acknowledging a payment, and a secondary 50 ms behind is elected. The payment is missing. What would have prevented the loss?
options: Reading with read concern majority, so that the client never sees a write that could be rolled back
Using w:all, so every node has the write before the acknowledgement and no election can lose it
Going from 3 nodes to 5, so the election is slower and the lagging secondary has time to catch up
Writing with w:majority, so the acknowledgement waits until most nodes hold the write
quiz.explanation: With w:majority, any node that can win an election holds the write. The journal only protects the old primary's own disk, and that node rolls the entry back when it returns. w:all would stall on one dead node, and read concern governs reads, not writes.
